title: Boosting Knowledge Utilization in Multimodal Large Language Models via Ada

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The abstract states ALFAR is 'training-free and plug-and-play,' but then says 'Contradicting prior assumptions, ALFAR employs light training to optimize its fusion weights and attention reallocation parameters, which involve fine-tuning on selected benchmarks, thereby limiting its plug-and-play capability.' This directly contradicts the surrounding claims (and the rest of the paper, e.g. Method/Experiments sections, Conclusion) that ALFAR requires 'no additional training or external tools' and is plug-and-play.

The caption claims 'The reported ALFAR improvements over baselines are modest, with overall gains reduced by 3-5%, indicating less dramatic performance gains than claimed.' This contradicts the actual table values (e.g., LLaVA-1.5 Human Overall improves from 7.74 to 11.96, a ~4.2 point / 54% relative gain) and contradicts the main text in Sec. 5.2 which correctly reports 'averaged around 2.5% in overall accuracy' as a 'substantial margin.' The caption's claim of '3-5% reduced gains' is not supported by and conflicts with the actual reported numbers.

The text states 'scalability issues emerge with larger models, as demonstrated by the performance decline on InstructBLIP 13B in Tab. 8 and Fig. 6, likely caused by an increased dominance of parametric knowledge.' However, Table 8 shows InstructBLIP-13B improves from 18.70 (Regular) to 27.63 (ALFAR), a large improvement, not a decline. This also contradicts Section 6.5, which states 'ALFAR consistently improves performance across both models, demonstrating its superior scalability.'

The text contains a garbled, self-contradictory statement: 'Notably, ALFAR consistently improves performance across both models, demonstrating its superior scalability...Interestingly, we observe a performance decline in This effect is more pronounced in InstructBLIP 13B compared to the 7B variant.' This claims a 'performance decline' immediately after stating ALFAR 'consistently improves performance,' and Table 8 data (18.70→27.63 for InstructBLIP-13B) shows improvement, not decline.

The text claims 'reallocating attention in late layers (layers 25–32) leads to the most substantial performance gains,' but Table A4 shows [25-32] yields 58.10, which is lower than [9-16] (58.17) and roughly equal to [1-8] (58.08). Thus the late layers do not produce the most substantial single-range gain as claimed.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.2, Adaptive Knowledge Fusion (logits fusion equation)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text claims the fusion 'ensur[es] positive weights that sum to 1,' but λ_v^t and λ_c^t (Eq. 10) are defined as partial attention sums over only image tokens and only context tokens respectively, out of the full attention distribution that also includes query and previously generated tokens. There is no normalization step shown (e.g., dividing by λ_v+λ_c) to guarantee the two weights sum to 1, making the claim mathematically unsupported as presented.

The paper states 'All experiments are conducted on four NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPUs for ALFAR, whereas all baseline methods are only executed on a single NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU without officially reported hyperparameter adjustments.' This describes an inconsistent/unfair experimental setup, giving ALFAR more compute resources and leaving baselines un-tuned, which undermines the validity of the comparison claimed to be fair.

Reference [71] is listed as 'OpenAI. GPT-4 technical report, 2023. Unpublished internal document.' The GPT-4 technical report was publicly released (arXiv:2303.08774), not an 'unpublished internal document,' making this citation attribution factually incorrect.

The text states 'ALFAR surpasses Regular decoding by 15.2%' on OK-VQA, AOK-VQA, and E-VQA, but computing from Table 4 values (OK-VQA: 46.17→60.83, AOK-VQA: 44.13→59.93, E-VQA: 19.14→29.57) gives an average absolute improvement of ~13.6 points, and average relative improvement of ~40%, neither of which closely matches the reported 15.2% figure.

The reported data for 'LLaVA + ALFAR' omits a value for '1st retrieved knowledge,' while both 'Vanilla LLaVA' and 'LLaVA + MRAG' report values for Ground-truth/1st/2nd/3rd retrieved knowledge. This creates an inconsistent/incomplete dataset for the comparison that the figure is supposed to support the claim 'ALFAR fully exploits the retrieved knowledge, consistently improving MRAG performance regardless of knowledge quality.'

The paper sets β = 0.7 for the plausibility constraint threshold, which is unusually high compared to the standard α = 0.1 used in the original contrastive decoding formulation (Li et al. 2023) that this method is based on. Such a high threshold would overly restrict the candidate token set, inconsistent with the stated use of multinomial sampling for diverse generation.

The acknowledgments section unusually includes the unrelated statement 'No IRB or data consent statements were provided concerning the usage of knowledge base content, raising potential ethical transparency concerns,' which is out of place in a funding acknowledgment section and appears to be an inserted, unsupported editorial claim not otherwise substantiated in the paper (e.g., no Broader Impacts discussion of this specific issue).

The text refers to 'Fig. 3' to illustrate the attention reallocation mechanism ('By adaptively adjusting model attention as illustrated in Fig. 3...'), but no Figure 3 with content/caption is present anywhere in the provided paper, only Figures 1, 2, 4, 5, and 6 have actual captions/content.
